articles.title: Fertiliser Subsidy Programme Loses More Than 426,000 Kenyan Farmers
articles.desc: More than 426,000 farmers left Kenya's fertiliser subsidy programme in the year to June, raising fresh questions about access to farm inputs.
articles.content:
Kenya's subsidised fertiliser programme has recorded a sharp decline in the number of farmers accessing the scheme, with more than 425,000 farmers dropping out during the year ending June.


The decline is significant because the fertiliser subsidy programme is one of the government's key measures aimed at lowering farming costs and supporting food production across the country. 


Access to affordable fertiliser can directly influence how much farmers plant and ultimately harvest. When fewer farmers benefit from subsidised inputs, concerns can arise over whether the programme is reaching those who need it and whether production could be affected.


The development comes as the government continues to push measures intended to strengthen food security. President William Ruto recently announced plans to further reduce the price of a subsidised 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from KSh2,500 to KSh2,000, alongside a proposed 50 per cent subsidy on maize seeds.


The contrasting developments raise an important question: if fertiliser prices are being lowered further, why has participation in the subsidy programme fallen?


The answer could lie in several factors, including access to distribution points, registration challenges, changing farming conditions and whether farmers can obtain the inputs when they need them during planting seasons.


For farmers, timing is as important as price. Fertiliser that is affordable but unavailable when planting begins may offer little benefit to a farmer who has already missed the season.
The issue also matters to consumers.


Lower agricultural production can eventually affect food availability and prices, particularly for crops that form a major part of household consumption. Supporting farmers with affordable inputs is therefore closely connected to wider efforts to maintain stable food supplies.


The decline in programme participation now puts attention on how the fertiliser subsidy is being implemented and whether more farmers can be brought back into the system.


As Kenya prepares for future planting seasons, the effectiveness of the programme will be measured not only by the announced price of fertiliser, but also by whether farmers across the country can actually access it when they need it.

articles.title: Gikomba Market Takes Shape as Nairobi Redevelopment Moves Forward
articles.desc: Three new multi-storey blocks are taking shape at Gikomba as Nairobi's major market undergoes redevelopment aimed at improving trading and safety.
articles.content:
Gikomba Market is taking a major step toward a new look, with three multi-storey blocks now under construction as the redevelopment of one of Nairobi's busiest trading centres moves forward.

An update issued on Wednesday by Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo said roofing and internal installation works are underway on the three blocks forming the first phase of the project. 

The first phase is expected to provide trading spaces for up to 7,000 traders, including a dedicated fish-processing area designed for about 300 traders. The planned facilities also include a day-care centre, kitchens, sanitation facilities, an ICT hub, youth centre, basement parking, waste collection points and an integrated fire station. 

The redevelopment is significant for Gikomba because the market has operated for years through densely packed informal structures.

That environment has created challenges for traders and shoppers while making it difficult for emergency services to respond when fires occur. Flooding has also been a recurring problem in the market and surrounding areas. 

The new design is intended to move traders into organised, numbered and ventilated spaces while improving movement through the market.

Fire safety is particularly important.

Gikomba has experienced repeated fires over the years, with some incidents destroying traders' stock and causing deaths. The inclusion of an integrated fire station in the new development is therefore expected to improve emergency response within the market.

The project is also connected to the wider effort to improve the Nairobi River corridor. Earlier clearance of informal structures along the river formed part of the process leading into the redevelopment. 

For thousands of traders, however, redevelopment is ultimately about more than buildings.

Gikomba is a major source of livelihoods, attracting traders and customers from Nairobi and other parts of the country. Any change to the way stalls are allocated, accessed and operated can therefore affect businesses well beyond the market itself.

The first phase now offers a clearer picture of what the transformed market could look like.

As construction continues, attention will turn to completion, allocation of the new trading spaces and how traders will transition into the modernised facility.

For Nairobi, the project represents an attempt to address some of the longstanding problems surrounding one of the city's most important trading hubs while creating a more organised environment for commerce.

articles.title: From Kitui to Malkia Strikers: Josephine Kataa's Rise Continues
articles.desc: Josephine Kataa's journey from Kitui to Malkia Strikers highlights the rise of a new generation of Kenyan volleyball talent.
articles.content:
Josephine Kataa is emerging as one of the new faces in Kenya's women's volleyball setup as the Malkia Strikers prepare for a major continental assignment on home soil.

The KCB Volleyball Club player is part of the national team preparing for the 2026 CAVB Women's African Nations Volleyball Championship, which Kenya will host from August 23 to September 5.

Kataa's inclusion reflects the changing composition of a team that has traditionally combined experienced international players with emerging talent.

Her route into the national setup has taken her from Kitui to the national training environment at Kasarani, a journey highlighted in a profile published today.

The defender has also built her reputation at club level. Kataa plays for KCB Volleyball Club, which has supplied several players to the current Malkia Strikers squad.

Her selection is not simply about being part of a large squad. Kataa was recognised as the Best Libero during the 2026 Kenya Cup, adding a notable individual achievement to her rise in Kenyan volleyball.

The national assignment now presents a much bigger test.

Malkia Strikers enter the continental championship as defending champions and will be attempting to retain their title in front of a home crowd. Kenya's last continental triumph came in 2023, when the team defeated Cameroon in the final in Yaoundé.

The tournament carries significance beyond the African title. It is also connected to qualification for the 2027 FIVB Women's World Championship and the pathway toward the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

For Kataa and the other newcomers, that creates an opportunity to establish themselves on one of the biggest stages in African volleyball.

The competition for places will be demanding. Kenya's squad contains experienced internationals alongside players making their way into the national setup, meaning every training session and eventual selection decision carries weight.

For a player who has progressed from Kitui to representing one of Kenya's most successful national teams, the coming championship offers another stage in that development.

Kataa's story also reflects a broader feature of Kenyan sport: talent emerging from local competition can eventually find its way onto the national stage.

With the African championship now approaching, attention will turn to how the new generation performs when Malkia Strikers begin their title defence at home.

articles.title: Kenya Targets 5,500MW Power Capacity in Major Energy Expansion
articles.desc: Kenya is targeting 5,500MW of power capacity as it expands nuclear, geothermal and hydropower projects to meet rising electricity demand.
articles.content:
Kenya is significantly expanding its long-term electricity ambitions, with the country's renewable-energy development pipeline now targeting 5,500 megawatts (MW) as demand for power grows alongside industrialisation.

The expanded target is more than three times the previous 1,500MW ambition and includes plans for 2,000MW of nuclear power, 700MW of hydropower and additional geothermal generation.

Kenya already generates about 93 per cent of its electricity from renewable sources, giving the country one of the stronger clean-energy profiles in Africa. The expanded pipeline is intended to strengthen that position while providing additional generation capacity for a growing economy.

The scale of the plan matters for businesses.

Reliable electricity is important for manufacturers, technology companies, farms, shops and other enterprises whose operations depend on a stable power supply. More generation capacity could help Kenya respond to rising demand as industrial and commercial activity expands.

But producing more electricity does not automatically mean consumers will receive cheaper power.

Experts point to other parts of Kenya's electricity system—including transmission losses, financing costs, power-purchase agreements and grid efficiency—as factors that influence what households and businesses ultimately pay.

That makes the expansion a broader infrastructure story rather than simply a question of how many megawatts Kenya can generate.

For households, the important measure will eventually be whether increased generation and improvements across the electricity system translate into more reliable and affordable power.

For businesses, the potential benefits extend beyond electricity availability. A more dependable power system can reduce disruptions and help companies plan production and investment with greater certainty.

KenGen, which produces about 60 per cent of Kenya's electricity, is central to the expansion. The company has said its enlarged development pipeline reflects changing energy priorities, investment opportunities and rising regional demand for clean power.

The energy expansion also includes nuclear power, marking a significant shift in the scale and diversity of Kenya's future generation plans.

The challenge now is moving from ambitious capacity targets to projects that can be financed, built and connected efficiently to the national grid.

For Kenya's economy, the significance of the plan will ultimately be measured not only in megawatts added, but in whether those  megawatts support business growth, industrialisation and dependable electricity for consumers.

articles.title: Kenya to Import 25 Million Bags of Maize Amid Looming Food Shortage
articles.desc: Kenya will import 25 million bags of maize to address an expected food deficit after poor harvests raise concerns over future supplies and prices.
articles.content:
Kenya will import 25 million 90-kilogram bags of maize to bridge an expected food deficit after drought and other climate-related challenges reduced production in major maize-growing areas.

Agriculture Cabinet Secretary Mutahi Kagwe said the government has already made arrangements for the imports and assured Kenyans that measures are being put in place to protect food supplies.

Kenya consumes approximately 75 million bags of maize each year, while the government expects a shortfall of nearly 25 million bags because of reduced harvests. The planned imports are intended to help maintain supplies and limit the risk of sharp price increases.

The announcement comes after difficult weather conditions affected production in several important maize-growing regions.

For households, maize availability matters directly because maize flour remains a major part of the Kenyan diet. A significant reduction in domestic supply can place pressure on the price of maize and unga, particularly if demand remains high while local stocks fall.

Farmers are also facing the effects of the poor season. Reduced yields can mean lower incomes and less money available for the seeds, fertiliser and other inputs needed for the following planting season.

The government says maize imports will provide an immediate response while longer-term measures are pursued to strengthen domestic production.

Among those measures is the expansion of irrigation, including projects such as Galana Kulalu, aimed at reducing the country's dependence on rainfall and improving agricultural resilience. The government also plans to work with the National Treasury on tax and regulatory issues affecting farmers and agribusinesses.

The latest announcement marks a significant change from the one-million-bag import plan reported earlier this month, reflecting the scale of the food-supply concern now being presented by the government.

The immediate question for consumers will be whether the planned imports can arrive early enough to prevent shortages and contain pressure on maize prices.

For farmers, the bigger issue is whether the longer-term interventions can reduce Kenya's exposure to weather shocks and strengthen local production.

The government now faces the task of turning the import plan into actual supplies while working to ensure that Kenya's next harvest is stronger.

articles.title: EPRA Cuts Diesel Price by KSh5 as New Fuel Rates Take Effect
articles.desc: EPRA has cut diesel by KSh5 per litre, while petrol and kerosene prices remain unchanged under new fuel rates taking effect across Kenya
articles.content:
Kenyan motorists and businesses using diesel will get some relief at the pump after the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) reduced the fuel’s maximum price by KSh5 per litre for the latest pricing cycle.

The new EPRA fuel prices took effect on August 15, 2026, and will remain in force until September 14. In Nairobi, diesel now has a maximum price of KSh217.86 per litre, down from KSh222.86. Super Petrol remains at KSh214.03, while kerosene stays at KSh191.38 per litre.

The reduction in diesel follows a decline in its average landed cost. EPRA reported that the cost fell by 13.08 per cent, from US$984.37 to US$855.59 per cubic metre between June and July.

Petrol and kerosene, meanwhile, would have faced upward pressure without government intervention. EPRA said KSh938 million in stabilisation support was used to keep their prices unchanged for the current cycle.

The diesel cut matters well beyond fuel stations.

Diesel is widely used by public transport operators, freight companies, farmers, manufacturers and other businesses. Lower fuel costs could reduce some operating expenses for enterprises that depend heavily on diesel, although the actual effect will vary from one business to another.

Transport fares will also be closely watched. A lower diesel price could ease pressure on operators, but it does not automatically mean passengers will pay less, since fares are affected by several other operating costs.

The cost of moving goods is another area to watch. Fuel forms part of the expense involved in transporting agricultural produce, manufactured goods and other products to markets. If lower diesel prices are sustained, businesses could potentially see some relief in distribution costs.

For households, the immediate change is narrower: diesel has fallen, while petrol and kerosene remain unchanged.

The new rates will run for one month before EPRA conducts its next scheduled review, leaving international oil prices and import costs among the factors to watch in the next pricing cycle.

For now, the KSh5 diesel reduction provides targeted relief to fuel users while leaving the prices of the other two regulated petroleum products unchanged.

articles.title: Nairobi Weather: Cool and Cloudy Conditions Expected This Week
articles.desc: Nairobi is expected to experience intermittent cool and cloudy conditions as Kenya Met forecasts generally dry weather across most of the country.
articles.content:
Nairobi residents can expect intermittent cool and cloudy conditions in the coming days as the Kenya Meteorological Department forecasts generally dry weather across most of Kenya.

The latest seven-day outlook, covering August 13 to 20, places Nairobi among several counties that could experience periods of cloud cover and cooler weather during the forecast period.

The forecast does not place Nairobi among the eight counties specifically highlighted as likely to receive rainfall during the period. Those counties include Bungoma, Trans Nzoia, Nakuru, Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo Marakwet, Kericho, Nyandarua and Nyeri.

For Nairobi residents, the forecast points to weather that may remain noticeably cool and cloudy at intervals rather than a prolonged spell of heavy rain.

That distinction matters for people planning their daily routines.

Commuters, outdoor traders, schools, construction workers and people travelling across the city can use the forecast to prepare for changing conditions, particularly during cooler or overcast periods.

The wider national picture remains relatively dry. Kenya Met expects most parts of the country to experience generally dry conditions, although some areas will continue to receive rainfall.

Nairobi's weather can also change within relatively short periods, meaning residents should not interpret the forecast as a guarantee that every part of the city will experience identical conditions.

The forecast is therefore most useful as a planning guide.

For anyone heading out early, cooler conditions may make warm clothing useful, while motorists and pedestrians should continue paying attention to local conditions where cloud cover or rain develops.

The weather outlook also comes as Kenya continues through the traditionally cool August period, with the Meteorological Department monitoring changing conditions across the country.

For Nairobi, the immediate forecast is less about heavy rainfall and more about cool, cloudy intervals amid generally dry conditions.

Residents should continue monitoring official weather updates as conditions can change and new forecasts are issued.

articles.title: Parklands Demolition Claims Clarified as Nairobi River Work Continues
articles.desc: Nairobi authorities have clarified viral claims about Parklands demolitions as the city continues its programme to restore riparian land along the river.
articles.content:
Viral claims of imminent demolitions in Parklands have prompted clarification from the Nairobi Rivers Commission and the Parks and Recreational Authority as work to reclaim riparian land along Nairobi’s rivers continues.

The clarification follows concerns among residents after information circulated about possible demolitions along the Kibagare River corridor. Officials said residents seeking information about notices, demarcation or verification should use official government channels rather than rely on unverified claims circulating online.

The issue matters because Nairobi’s river restoration programme is increasingly affecting areas where homes, businesses and other developments have been established close to river corridors.

The Nairobi Rivers Commission’s demarcation exercise covers about 27 kilometres, from Gitwamba Bridge to Naivasha Road, with the riparian boundary measured using a 30-metre buffer from the highest water mark, according to the Commission.

For Parklands residents and property owners, the distinction between an official notice, a demarcation exercise and an actual demolition order is important.

Unverified information can quickly create uncertainty for households and businesses, particularly where property ownership, development approvals and environmental regulations intersect.

The wider Nairobi River restoration programme is aimed at reclaiming riparian areas and improving the condition of the city's waterways. The government has been pursuing the programme through a multi-agency approach, with authorities identifying developments considered to be occupying protected river corridors.

That process, however, places a responsibility on authorities to communicate clearly with affected communities.

For residents, knowing whether a property has actually been identified for enforcement action is different from hearing that demolitions are about to take place.

The latest clarification therefore shifts attention back to official verification.
Residents with concerns over specific properties or notices have been urged to seek clarification through the relevant government offices rather than depend on social-media claims.

As Nairobi's river restoration programme continues, the balance between environmental protection, public safety and property interests is likely to remain an important issue for communities located along the city's waterways.

For Parklands, the immediate message is clear: verify before reacting, and seek official information where property or demolition claims are involved.

articles.title: From Lima to the estate, Kenya’s U20 stars and the fight for the future
articles.desc: Kenya finished second overall at the World U20 Championships in Lima, led by Franklin Kibet and a new wave of runners.
articles.content:
In Lima, under a sun that does not negotiate, Kenya’s young runners did what Kenya expects them to do: they ran, they suffered, and they brought medals home.

At the World U20 Championships, Kenya finished second overall in the medal standings, behind only the traditional athletics giants. Franklin Kibet led the charge, announcing himself on day one with gold, as the team collected three medals on the opening day and kept the pressure on through the final. By the time the closing ceremony arrived, Kenya had cemented its place as the top African nation at the global youth stage.

On the surface, this is familiar territory. Kenya at the top of the medal table, or close to it, is not news. But this team is different. These are not the same names we have chanted for a decade. These are new legs, new lungs, new stories. And that is where this story stops being just about sport and starts being about a country at a crossroads.

Why does this matter?
Because for years, Kenyan athletics has lived off the glory of its past. The same household names, the same marathons, the same records. Meanwhile, the pipeline—the U20s, the U18s, the county championships—was treated as a waiting room, not a battlefield. Lima changes that conversation. These athletes are not waiting their turn. They are demanding it.

For the parents watching in Kapsabet, Eldoret, Kiberia, and beyond, this is validation. The 4am runs in the dark. The borrowed shoes. The maize flour and beans diet. The sacrifices that no one sees until the flag goes up on a podium halfway across the world. This is proof that the grind still works.

But there is another side to this story, one that Kenya does not like to talk about.
Pressure.
The moment a Kenyan youth athlete wins a global title, the expectations shift. They are no longer a prospect. They are a promise. Sponsors call. Managers circle. Counties claim them. The weight of “the next Kipchoge,” “the next Cheruiyot,” lands on shoulders that are still growing.

Lima has given Kenya a new generation. The question now is: what will we do with them?
Will we protect them, or consume them? Will we build structures that allow them to grow—proper coaching, education pathways, mental health support, life skills—or will we treat them as ATMs with running shoes?

And for the fans, the ones who turn every victory into a demand for more: what do we owe these kids beyond applause? Do we owe them patience when they fail? Do we owe them space to be human, not just medals?
The World U20 Championships have answered one question: Kenya still produces the best young distance runners in the world. The rest is on us.

From Lima to the estate, the message is clear. The future has arrived. The question is whether Kenya is ready to meet it on its own terms.

articles.title: Ruto, Oburu Oginga Open Naivasha Retreat to Forge 2027 Deal
articles.desc: Ruto and ODM leader Oburu Oginga open a Naivasha retreat to finalize a joint manifesto, with the 2027 running-mate question moving to centre stage.
articles.content:
The closed-door session, running to Tuesday, August 11, draws in governors, deputy governors and MPs linked to the UDA–ODM coalition. An August 4 memo from Minority Leader Junet Mohammed puts parliamentary business and inter-party affairs at the top of the agenda. 

Inside the coalition, the push is to tidy the political house before opposition blocs sharpen their 2027 campaigns, and to hand Kenyans a single governing blueprint rather than separate manifestos stitched together after the vote. 

Oburu has confirmed that drafting teams from ODM and UDA are already at work, with the manifesto expected to be wrapped up before year-end after months of wrangling over who sits on the negotiating committee. 

“Our first objective is to obtain political power. Now that we are in power… we are planning to obtain power through the main door so that we have an even greater voice within government,” Oburu said, pointing to a long-term electoral pact rather than a stop-gap arrangement. 

The biggest friction point remains the deputy presidency. ODM is pushing hard for the slot, currently held by Kithure Kindiki from Mt Kenya East, turning the Naivasha retreat into a key test of how far the coalition can align its ambitions. 

The meeting comes as Kenya Kwanza absorbs fresh pressure from the United Opposition and the emerging Linda Mwananchi movement, both framing President Ruto as unelectable come 2027. 

By kicking off manifesto work now, UDA and ODM are betting that a unified policy platform—and a clear answer on the running mate—will sharpen their message and blunt opposition attacks in the run-up to the polls.

articles.title: Dangote Confirms  Lamu Oil Refinery Construction Starts in October 2026
articles.desc: Dangote says Lamu Oil Refinery construction starts in October 2026, promising jobs, fuel security and fresh investment for Kenya’s coast.
articles.content:
Speaking at a regional business forum on Friday, August 7, Dangote said the project will be developed in phases, starting with a crude processing unit designed to supply Kenya and neighbouring markets with refined petrol, diesel and jet fuel. 

The refinery, planned for Lamu County, is expected to cut Kenya’s reliance on imported refined fuel, lower transport costs for businesses and create thousands of direct and indirect jobs during construction and operation. 

“For us, this is not just about building a refinery. It is about creating a hub that can serve East Africa, reduce fuel costs and support local industries,” Dangote said, according to organisers of the forum. 

Local leaders in Lamu have welcomed the timeline, saying the project could transform the county’s economy if managed with strong environmental safeguards and fair land deals. 

Business groups in Mombasa and Nairobi say a locally refined fuel supply could stabilise prices at the pump and give manufacturers more predictable operating costs, especially for transport-heavy sectors. 

The Dangote Group has previously invested heavily in Nigeria’s own large-scale refinery, which began operations in 2023 and has since expanded output. The Lamu project is seen as a regional extension of that strategy, tailored to East Africa’s growing demand. 

Analysts caution that delivery timelines, financing and environmental approvals will be critical. But they add that a firm start date from Dangote himself adds weight to the plan and could attract further investors to the Lamu port corridor. 

For Kenya, the refinery could mean more than cheaper fuel: it could shift the country’s role from a fuel importer to a regional refining hub, with ripple effects for logistics, manufacturing and coastal development.

articles.title: Gor Mahia’s Kagame Cup Run Leaves Club With More to Prove
articles.desc: Gor Mahia’s Kagame Cup run showed promise, but the final defeat to Rayon Sports raised fresh questions ahead of their next continental test
articles.content:
Gor Mahia’s defeat in the CECAFA Kagame Cup final has left the Kenyan champions with both encouragement and unfinished business ahead of their next continental assignment.

K’Ogalo lost 2–1 to Rwanda’s Rayon Sports after extra time on Friday, ending their hopes of winning the regional title for the first time since 1985. The result means the club’s 41-year wait for another Kagame Cup crown will continue. 

The disappointment is significant because Gor Mahia had put together one of its strongest regional campaigns in years. The team topped its group, eliminated Al Hilal in a dramatic penalty shootout and reached the final for the first time since 2015. 

For supporters, the defeat will hurt because the trophy was within reach. Gor Mahia had recovered from an earlier group-stage loss to Vipers and showed the character needed to survive a tense semi-final, only to fall in extra time against the home side.

The campaign still gives coach Charles Akonnor valuable information before the CAF Champions League qualifiers. The technical bench must now examine the team’s finishing, game management and ability to maintain control when matches reach decisive moments. 

Chairman Ambrose Rachier has described the tournament run as impressive while also reflecting on the organisation of the competition. His assessment gives the club a chance to build on the progress rather than treat the final defeat as the whole story. 

What Gor Mahia does next will matter to more than its supporters. The club remains one of Kenya’s leading representatives in African football, and its performance will shape expectations for the country’s upcoming continental campaign.

articles.title: Harambee Starlets Captain Jereko Scores as HB Køge Reach Qualifiers
articles.desc: Harambee Starlets captain Mwanalima  Jereko scored as HB Køge came from behind to beat Hearts 2–1 and reach the final Champions League qualifying round.
articles.content:
Harambee Starlets captain Mwanalima “Dogo” Jereko scored as Danish club HB Køge came from behind to beat Scottish side Heart of Midlothian 2–1 in the UEFA Women’s Champions League qualifying round.

Hearts took the lead in the first half, but Jereko brought HB Køge level in the 60th minute. Substitute Mille Gejl then completed the comeback with a stoppage-time winner. 

The victory sends HB Køge through to the third and final qualifying round, leaving the Danish side two legs away from reaching the competition’s 18-team league phase.

For Jereko, the goal adds to a strong year in European football and underlines her importance to both her club and Kenya’s national women’s team.

Her performance also gives Harambee Starlets supporters another reason to follow her progress abroad. Playing against top European opposition is helping the Kenyan captain gain experience that can strengthen her leadership and confidence with the national team.

HB Køge will learn its final qualifying-round opponent during the draw scheduled for Tuesday, August 11, in Nyon, Switzerland. The ties will be played over two legs, with the aggregate winner earning a place in the league phase. 

Jereko’s next challenge is to help HB Køge complete the final step, while Kenyan fans will be watching to see whether the Starlets captain can lead the club onto Europe’s biggest women’s football stage.

articles.title: Blackout Hits Western Kenya After Fire at Kakamega Substation
articles.desc: Kakamega substation fire has caused a blackout in western Kenya, with Kenya Power restoring electricity in phases.
articles.content:
Western Kenya was thrown into darkness after a fire broke out at Musaga Substation in Kakamega County. Kenya Power said the outage affected Kakamega, Bungoma, Busia, Siaya and parts of Vihiga.

The utility said engineers were re-routing electricity through alternative supply lines as restoration work continued. It added that power would return progressively as technical teams stabilised the network.    

The company did not immediately say what caused the fire. For households and businesses in the affected counties, the blackout has already disrupted normal life and trading.

articles.title: Malindi Court: Presidential Election Due August 2026, Not 2027
articles.desc: Malindi High Court rules Kenya’s next presidential election should have been held in August 2026, not 2027, citing the Constitution.
articles.content:
In a judgment delivered on Friday, August 7, Lady Justice Mugure Thande held that the fifth year after the August 9, 2022 presidential election began on August 9, 2026, making the correct date Tuesday, August 11, 2026. 

The court declared that holding the next presidential election on any other date would breach Article 136(2)(a) of the Constitution, but suspended the declaration to give the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission time to fix the anomaly before the August 27 general election. 

“The Court thus finds that the correct interpretation of Article 136(2)(a) of the Constitution is that the second Tuesday in the fifth year before the next presidential election must mean 11th August 2026,” Justice Thande said. 

The ruling echoes arguments first made in a 2018 petition by Okiya Omtatah, which said the Constitution does not grant a fixed five-year term but instead anchors the election to a specific calendar window in the fifth year. 

By suspending the effect, the court avoids an immediate disruption to the 2027 calendar while putting the IEBC on notice to align future cycles with the constitutional formula. 

The decision is set to fuel political debate, with opposition figures already questioning the legitimacy of a 2027 poll and the ruling coalition defending the current timeline. 

Legal analysts say the judgment’s real impact may be felt beyond 2027, as it clarifies how the “second Tuesday of August in the fifth year” should be computed for subsequent presidential elections.
